ndss.narrative:
Digital forensics and provenance-based detection at NDSS has undergone a dramatic evolution from log collection toward real-time, ML-assisted threat detection. Fear and Logging in the Internet of Things (NDSS 2018) highlighted the glaring absence of forensic infrastructure in IoT ecosystems. NoDoze (NDSS 2019) took the first major step forward by using automated provenance triage to combat alert fatigue, showing that causal graphs over audit logs could dramatically cut investigation time.

Unicorn (NDSS 2020) extended provenance-based detection to advanced persistent threats, demonstrating that long-running attacks leave causality signatures recoverable from streaming graphs. WATSON (NDSS 2021) complemented this by abstracting coarse behaviors from fine-grained audit logs, reducing the semantic gap between raw telemetry and analyst-interpretable incidents.

By 2022–2025 the field had integrated large models and begun tackling adversarial forensics. Interpretable Federated Transformer Log Learning (NDSS 2022) applied transformer architectures to cloud threat forecasting in a federated setting; BEAGLE (NDSS 2023) studied how forensic techniques can characterize deep-learning backdoor attacks; and VoiceRadar (NDSS 2025) showed that voice deepfake detection can be framed as a forensic micro-frequency analysis problem. The trajectory is clear: provenance graphs and ML are becoming inseparable from modern forensic pipelines.

uss.narrative:
The earliest work in this collection, all from USENIX 2018, set the agenda for modern digital forensics: making attack investigation scale to the kind of long-running campaigns that hide in months of audit logs. "Dependence-Preserving Data Compaction for Scalable Forensic Analysis" (USENIX 2018) attacked the sheer volume problem by shrinking provenance data without losing the causal dependencies investigators need, while "SAQL: A Stream-based Query System for Real-Time Abnormal System Behavior Detection" (USENIX 2018) pushed toward catching abnormal behavior as it happened rather than after the fact. "Enabling Refinable Cross-Host Attack Investigation with Efficient Data Flow Tagging and Tracking" (USENIX 2018) broadened the lens from a single machine to multi-host campaigns, recovering true cross-host dependencies. Alongside system-log forensics, this period also seeded the memory-forensics thread, with "Back to the Whiteboard" (USENIX 2019) calling for a more principled, evaluable foundation for memory analysis techniques.

Around 2020-2021 the field both diversified and embraced learning. "From Control Model to Program: Investigating Robotic Aerial Vehicle Accidents with MAYDAY" (USENIX 2020) extended forensics into cyber-physical accident reconstruction for drones. A 2021 USENIX cohort then matured the provenance-and-log line on several fronts at once: "ATLAS" introduced sequence-based learning to reconstruct attack stories from logs, "SEAL" and "ELISE" tackled storage-efficient causality analysis and logging through compression and representation learning, "CLARION" brought sound provenance tracking to containerized microservices, and "ARCUS" used symbolic execution for root-cause analysis of exploits in production. The same year showed the area's breadth, with malware-capability forecasting from memory images, YARA-based malware intelligence (YARIX), SDN causal analysis, and even physical-world tracing via Moiré patterns (mID).

By 2022-2023 forensics followed computing into new deployment models and confronted the human and adversarial realities of incident response. "ALASTOR: Reconstructing the Provenance of Serverless Intrusions" (USENIX 2022) carried provenance into serverless platforms, while case studies like "The Antrim County 2020 Election Incident" (USENIX 2022) and "Anatomy of a High-Profile Data Breach" (USENIX 2023) grounded the field in real investigations. Learning-driven and cost-aware detection advanced through "DISTDET" and the log-text unsupervised approach "AIRTAG" (both USENIX 2023), and "The Case for Learned Provenance Graph Storage Systems" (USENIX 2023) reframed even storage as a learning problem. Crucially, several 2023 papers turned the lens on the auditing pipeline itself, hardening it against attackers who compromise the OS or starve the audit framework ("Rethinking System Audit Architectures," "Auditing Frameworks Need Resource Isolation"), and "Lessons Lost" (USENIX 2023) examined how cyber insurance and breach attorneys distort incident response in practice.

Most recently, in 2024, the frontier moved toward forensics in adversarial and AI-laden environments. "00SEVen" (USENIX 2024) re-enabled VM forensics inside confidential VMs whose hardware protections otherwise block inspection, and "AI Psychiatry: Forensic Investigation of Deep Learning Networks in Memory Images" (USENIX 2024) opened the investigation of deployed neural networks recovered from memory. A parallel deepfake-forensics thread runs from vocal-tract-based detection (USENIX 2022) to a SoK measuring structural limits of deepfake datasets (USENIX 2024). Taken together, the area has grown from scaling system-log provenance to a multi-front discipline spanning memory, cyber-physical, serverless, confidential-computing, and ML-model forensics, increasingly defending the trustworthiness of the evidence itself.

top4.narrative:
The earliest cluster of work here, all from 2018, established the core problem of digital forensics in modern systems: how to record and reason about what happened on a machine after an intrusion. Several NDSS and USENIX papers attacked the fundamental scaling bottleneck of causality analysis -- audit logs grow enormous, so "Dependence-Preserving Data Compaction for Scalable Forensic Analysis" (USENIX 2018) and "NodeMerge" (CCS 2018) focused on shrinking provenance data without losing the dependencies investigators need, while "SAQL" (USENIX 2018) and "Towards a Timely Causality Analysis for Enterprise Security" (NDSS 2018) pushed toward real-time querying of behavior. Others broadened the setting: "Fear and Logging in the Internet of Things" (NDSS 2018) brought provenance to smart homes, "Runtime Analysis of Whole-System Provenance" (CCS 2018) made whole-system capture practical, and "Enabling Refinable Cross-Host Attack Investigation" (USENIX 2018) extended tracking across machines. A recurring theme was the "dependence explosion" problem -- single processes touching so many objects that the causal graph becomes uselessly dense.

The big shift in 2019-2020 was from raw forensic reconstruction toward detection and triage built on provenance. "HOLMES" (S&P 2019) and "NoDoze" (NDSS 2019) reframed provenance graphs as a live signal for spotting APTs and cutting alert fatigue, and "POIROT" (CCS 2019) introduced graph alignment to match observed behavior against threat-intelligence queries. "Unicorn" (NDSS 2020) and "You Are What You Do" (NDSS 2020) pushed runtime, provenance-based APT detection, while "Tactical Provenance Analysis" (S&P 2020) tied this directly to commercial EDR workflows. At the same time, researchers attacked two persistent weaknesses: dependence explosion (via new tag-propagation semantics in "Combating Dependence Explosion," S&P 2020, and layered log analysis in "OmegaLog," NDSS 2020) and log integrity itself -- "Custos" (NDSS 2020) and "Logging to the Danger Zone" (CCS 2020) recognized that audit logs are worthless if an attacker who owns the host can tamper with them.

From 2021 onward the field leaned heavily into machine learning and semantic abstraction to make forensic output usable by humans. "ATLAS" (USENIX 2021) cast attack investigation as sequence learning, "WATSON" (NDSS 2021) abstracted low-level events into higher-level behaviors, and a wave of graph-learning systems -- "SHADEWATCHER" (S&P 2022), "DEPCOMM" (S&P 2022), "ProvG-Searcher" (CCS 2023), and "Flash" (S&P 2024) -- applied recommendation, summarization, and graph representation learning to threat analysis. "AIRTAG" (USENIX 2023) even brought log-text language models into investigation, and "DISTDET" (USENIX 2023) tackled cost-effective distributed detection. The 2023 SoK, "History is a Vast Early Warning System" (S&P 2023), consolidated this decade of provenance-based auditing into a coherent framework. A few entries in the list sit slightly apart from the provenance mainline -- "BFT Protocol Forensics" (CCS 2021) on consensus accountability, and media-forensics work like audio-deepfake detection (USENIX 2022) and "DE-FAKE" (CCS 2023) -- reflecting how broadly "forensics" now spans, but the dominant arc is clear: from scalable logging, to provenance-based detection, to ML-driven, human-interpretable attack reconstruction.
